whatTheyArgued: The attached snip is Natyashastra 28.1-2 as quoted by Fox Strangways as an example of the sloka metre (prosody illustration, not a definition of tala). Read as a verse, it sorts instruments into four classes (tata stringed, avanaddha drums, ghana, susira wind) and glosses ghana as talas, i.e. cymbals/clappers in that verse. Fox Strangways separately treats musical time as derived from the prosody of verse; modern accounts define tala as a metric cycle of beats (avartana) distinct from raga. Natyashastra-tradition talas are built of laghu, guru, pluta units.

scholarship.supports: tala is a quantitative rhythm system rooted in Vedic/Sanskrit phonetic structure; sources include Natyashastra
scholarship.disputes: abstract only; says Indian tala is a different type of rhythm than European measure

bends.ours: File header opens 'Tala speaks:' with this verse, and says it embodies rhythm as independent of content.
bends.theirs: The verse classifies instruments; 'talas' there names the cymbal class. It does not state tala as a cycle independent of content.

bends.ours: 'A meter is a prior about time, not about what happens within it' (compendium work).
bends.theirs: I did not verify that any source says this. Fox Strangways argues the reverse direction: musical time develops from verse prosody and the language's structure.

bends.theirs: Tala is a cyclic measure of beats with sam/khali structure in music; there is no cycle or beat in our measure.
